coverage: Tuesday 18 August, complete in both Asia and the US. Xiaomi's results — the book's live event — landed after the HK close and are read from the company's own presentation. Written 08:05 SGT, before this morning's Asia open, so Xiaomi's price reaction is NOT in here. Prices and the release calendar were fetched deterministically in code; 6 agents did the narrative.
tldr: FIRST, A CORRECTION TO YESTERDAY'S BRIEF. I told you gold broke out to a new high on Monday and held it. That was wrong. A futures contract rolled underneath the symbol and Monday's close was rewritten from 4,479.50 to 4,417.80 — proven by volume collapsing from 4,739 to 673, and refuted independently by GLD, which cannot roll and rose only 1.00%. Monday's high never cleared the 13 August peak. So gold has now FAILED at its highs four consecutive sessions, not three-then-a-breakout. Three other Monday figures were wrong the same way: Brent 91.11 should have been 90.87, WTI 84.95 should have been 84.50, and silver's bar carried volume ZERO.

TUESDAY WAS A GLOBAL DURATION SHOCK, and it explains almost everything else. The US 30-year touched 5.32%, its highest since 2007, and Japan's 10-year hit 2.945% — a level unseen since SEPTEMBER 1996. Silver fell 3.58% against gold's 1.71%, more than double, with the dollar FLAT and no silver-specific driver findable anywhere. That is a real-rate shock hitting the most leveraged non-yielding asset first: roughly -5.7% on your 1.6x position, the worst session of the run.

THE STRUCTURAL POINT UNDERNEATH IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: this long-end move is supply-driven, not growth-driven. Corporate issuance is running near $1.7 trillion year-to-date, up 27%, and technology alone has sold roughly $192bn of bonds through late July against $61bn five years ago. AI capital spending is being funded in the bond market and is crowding out duration globally. That will not resolve on a soft inflation print — and Tuesday proved it again, with housing starts collapsing 12.4% and long yields rising anyway. Three consecutive soft US prints, zero duration relief.

XIAOMI REPORTED: revenue -6.1%, adjusted profit -42.6%, and NO interim dividend — the board notice had said 'if any', so it was a genuine open question and the answer is no. Smartphone gross margin fell to just 8.5% on component costs and shipments dropped 26.3%, though ASP hit a record RMB1,351 (+25.9%) on premium mix. Against the one preview I could verify, adjusted profit actually BEAT by 5.7%. The EV arm lost RMB2.6bn at the operating line — a loss that widened roughly eightfold year-on-year, though it narrowed from Q1. Your 26,662 shares rose 1.16% Tuesday BEFORE the numbers, so the whole reaction is this morning.

BARRICK FELL 7.82% AND I CANNOT TELL YOU WHY. There is no company news dated Tuesday anywhere in the public record; every verifiable catalyst is a week old. The price itself checks out — volume 402,704 was normal and the intraday range genuine, opening 44.75 and trading down to 41.78. A 7.8% move on normal volume with no identifiable cause deserves more of your attention than one with an obvious explanation. I would rather say the cause is unknown than supply a plausible-sounding one.

Equities sorted by LEVERAGE AND DURATION rather than sector: Nasdaq -1.33% and Russell -1.30% against the Dow's -0.22%, with PHLX semiconductors down as much as 5% intraday — Intel -6%, Micron -5%, Sandisk -6%. That is the first real reversal in the AI-hardware complex after last week's melt-up, and it is the read-across to watch for SMIC at this morning's open.

Energy was the ONLY major sleeve that worked: XLE +1.76% against USO +0.28%, on Iran and Hormuz supply risk after Monday's MOU expiry. Equities outperforming the commodity says the market is pricing sustained prices into earnings rather than a spot spike. A Ukrainian-drone explanation circulating for the move was refuted and struck.

SINGAPORE — and note the difference from yesterday: OCBC's -1.90% is a REAL decline. Its 47 cents went ex on MONDAY, so Monday's headline -0.76% was actually a 0.73% gain. Tuesday has no such excuse. DBS -1.51%. Both fell with the long end near post-2007 highs, which is the wrong direction for the usual 'banks like higher rates' reflex.
whatChanged: CORRECTION published as its own item, not quietly restated: four commodity figures in yesterday's brief were wrong because a futures contract rolled. Gold's Monday 'breakout' did not happen.

METHOD: all metals and energy percentages now come from ETF proxies. The futures series on this feed was found to carry gold volumes in the hundreds and to repeat identical volumes across different sessions.

TOOLING: added a revision detector that flags any closed session whose price changes between runs; a thin-bar gate for implausible volumes; trust flags routing to ETF proxies; and a validator that refuses to reconcile against a distrusted series. The detector itself had a bug — it wrote the file before reading the 'previous' run, so it diffed today against itself — found by testing it on this exact event.
Regime: "Gold finally held a breakout" → "A global duration shock — and gold never broke out after all"; risk-on 49% → 45%.
Barrick's 7.82% fall published as UNEXPLAINED. A claimed institutional revolt over dilution was struck when its source returned 403.
Xiaomi's EV segment framing corrected during verification: the RMB2.6bn operating loss widened ~8x from a prior-year LOSS of RMB0.3bn — it was not a swing from profit, as first drafted.

signals: The most useful thing I can tell you today is that I got yesterday wrong and how. A contract roll silently rewrote a published price, and the fix is now structural — a revision detector, volume gates, trust flags and ETF routing. But treat every commodity figure from before 19 August in this dashboard with suspicion; they came through the same unguarded path.

Gold failing four consecutive times at its highs, while the long end sits at post-2007 levels, is a coherent and uncomfortable picture: the debasement bid keeps appearing and keeps being overwhelmed by real rates. Your silver is the leveraged expression of the losing side of that fight, and Tuesday cost 5.7%.

The supply story is the one to internalise. AI capex has moved onto the bond market — $192bn of technology issuance against $61bn five years ago — which means the thing driving your equity gains is also driving the duration shock hurting your metals and REITs. Those are not separate exposures; they are two ends of the same trade.

Barrick is the item I would act on informationally rather than financially: find out what happened before deciding anything. A 7.8% drop on normal volume with a genuine intraday range and no public cause is a signal that someone knows something, or that a large holder is exiting.

Note the discipline that OCBC now demonstrates in both directions: Monday's -0.76% headline was really +0.73% once the 47c dividend was adjusted, and Tuesday's -1.90% is real with no such excuse. Getting this wrong in either direction misreads the bank — and both mechanical adjustments are now behind you.
